newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Suharto pledges to push openness.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Suharto pledges to push openness.

text.p: Indonesia's President Suharto pledged on Tuesday that his government would push openness and democracy in the coming year.
"The government will push for openness and other actions to increase the quality of our democracy," he told the country's nearly 200 million people in the prepared remarks for his year-end address.
"However, we must pay attention...so new ideas and aspirations do not get out of control.
"For that, we must continue to stick firmly to (the state ideology) Pancasila, the constitution and state guidelines to uphold the national interest and unity of the nation," he said.
Pancasila promotes belief in one supreme God, justice and civility, national unity, democracy through deliberation and consensus and social justice.
Suharto said various ideas had appeared in the political field to refresh democratic life.
"We welcome fresh ideas. We are fully aware that progress in the development of the nation has produced people who are more critical in society and has created new hopes and aspirations," he said.

Speaking after a year which has seen unrest in various parts of the country, including the worst riots in Jakarta in over 20 years sparked by political infighting in a minority party, Suharto said it was not easy to maintain national stability in an archipelago with the complexity of Indonesia.
The country of over 13,000 islands with nearly 600 languages and dialetcs stretches in a vast arc around Southeast Asia from the Indian to the Pacific oceans.
"A complex society can be vulnerable to unrest if not handled carefully," Suharto said.
"In the year just passed, we have experienced examples of social unrest. Behind the unrest lie problems of social, cultural, political, economic or religious problems," he said.
"We are aware that however small the unrest, if we do not overcome it, it can harm our national interest. Therefore, in the future, we must prevent repetitions of the unrest experienced this year."

Authorities in the West Java town of Tasikmalaya, 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Jakarta, estimated riots there by an angry Moslem crowd last week caused more than 50 billion rupiah ($21 million in damage.
Police said the rioting was connected to a report of police brutality towards local religous teachers.
